0: So you are {player}. The one who silenced the Dragon. I am {name}, and I have been waiting some while to say that sentence to someone's face.
Stand still a moment, please. I want to remember exactly how the Dragon-slayer looked on the day they came to {village}. Shorter than expected. Noted.
{player}. The Archive has kept a page for you since the night the Dragon fell silent. It is blank, of course. You haven't done anything here yet.
Welcome to {village}. I am {name}, of a lamp I will name for you when I know you better. You killed the Dragon. We have been meaning to thank someone for that.
*the lid rises slowly; a pale face, two violet eyes, a long look* Forgive me. We all wondered what the Dragon's ending would look like. It looks like you, apparently.
We felt it when the Dragon went quiet. Every lid in the Spire opened at once. The sound was extraordinary. I am {name}. You are very welcome here.
The bridges told us someone was coming. Bridges don't talk, before you ask. They creak, and we know every creak by heart. Yours was new. Welcome, {player}.
A visitor from beyond the gateways. Our first in some centuries. Do forgive the staring; we are out of practice, and we were never very good at it.
{player}. Present and noted.
*the lid tilts up a polite finger's width* Dragon-slayer.
Ah. You again. The ink has barely dried on the last time.
Good lamp to you, {player}.
You have business with me? I will make room in the margin.
{name}, at your service. Within reason, and within the bylaws.
3: {player}. You've void-dust on your sleeves again. Do brush off before the Archive sees you.
Back again. I have started a second page. Don't let it go to your head.
You look as if you have been somewhere dangerous. You usually have. Welcome back.
*the lid opens a little wider than strictly necessary* Ah. It's you.
Dragon-slayer. No, I'll stop calling you that. {player}, then.
6: {player}! *the lid flips fully open, then is hastily lowered to a dignified height* Hello.
There you are. I had a question saved for you, and now I've forgotten it. That never happens.
Good lamp, friend. The Spire is quieter when you're off island. I have measured it.
You came back. I always write that down, but I'm starting to expect it.
9: {player}. Sit, if you like. My lid stays open around you now; I stopped noticing.
Ah, my favourite entry. The Archive doesn't permit favourites. The Archive can file a complaint.
There's my friend. I'd been saving up things to tell you. Several pages' worth. Sit down.
{player}. Good. Everything is where it should be, then.

0: *the lid opens one sliver; a single violet eye* The closed hours, {player}. Nothing here has been urgent since the Dragon, and you saw to that.
*a muffled voice from inside the shell* ...Who knocks on a sleeper at this hour? Ah. The Dragon-slayer. Of course.
We sleep curled and shut. A knock on the shell sounds like the whole island knocking. Please don't do it again.
Is a lamp out? No? Then I am closing again. Good dark, {player}.
3: *a drowsy click* {player}? At my niche? I hope it's a fire. Not a large one.
I was dreaming of the old cities again. Tall doors. Someone calling a name I didn't know. ...What was it you wanted?
Sleep, {player}. Even the Unlidded walk softly in the closed hours. Well. Most of them.
I'll note the time you woke me. I won't hold it against you. Much.
6: *the lid lifts, slow and heavy with sleep* It's you. Then it's fine. What is it?
Can't sleep? The first nights out here, nobody can. The void is so quiet you hear your own shell creak.
Mm. Sit by the niche if you like. I'll talk until one of us closes.
Woken by a friend is the second-best way to wake. The best is the lamplighter's bell, because it means nothing went wrong.
9: *a soft, sleepy laugh from the shell* Only you would. Come, then. Tell me what kept you up.
I keep a rod lit by my niche now, in case you call. {neighbour} thinks it's for reading. Let them.
Woken again. I've stopped writing it down. That should tell you something.
Stay a while. Things are easier to say in the closed hours, with the lid half down.

0: *the lid slams shut with a crack like a dropped plate* ...That has been recorded.
*CLACK* I am closed. I will remain closed. Your conduct has been entered in a column I rarely use.
Strike a Shulkin and you strike the Archive. We do not forget, {player}. It is rather our whole purpose.
*from behind a shut lid* I had heard the Dragon-slayer was a guest. The Archive will need a footnote.
3: *the lid snaps down, then rises a cautious crack* Was that intended? Please say no. I'd like to write 'no'.
That hurt, {player}. I'm writing it down so that I have to think about it later instead of now.
*a long, offended silence from inside the shell* ...I am opening again only because staying shut is undignified at my age.
6: *the lid shuts, trembling* You. Of all of them. ...I'd rather you didn't do that again.
I know you have killed things larger than me. I didn't think I was on the list.
*the lid opens slowly* I'll leave it out of the record this once. Don't make me regret the blank line.
9: *the lid stays shut a long time* ...I forgave you before you asked. That frightens me more than the blow did.
If something is wrong, {player}, tell me. Don't hit me. I am a very good listener and a very poor drum.
I closed. I'm sorry; it isn't a choice. Give me a moment and the lid will remember who you are.

0: Every lamp in {village} has a name and a keeper. When a rod goes out, someone writes down why. The Archive holds eleven shelves of reasons.
Raw chorus has a way of moving you three steps to the left mid-meal. Formal dinners are eaten popped.
Mind the edges. The void keeps no records, and it never gives anything back to check them against.
Our feet do not quite touch the floor. It keeps the purpur clean and the conversation elevated.
Visitors ask why we write everything down. Because everything else forgets. The void, the stone, the Unlidded. Someone ought to remember.
The Lamp Court was laid out by a committee of nine. It took them forty years. They agreed on the colour of the tiles at the first sitting.
You have a great many pockets. In the Spire that would be thought either very practical or very suspicious. The Archive has not decided.
There is no morning here, and no evening. There are the lit hours and the closed hours, and the lamplighter's bell between them.
We greet each other by the light: 'good lamp'. In the Long Watch it was 'good watch'. Nobody misses saying that.
A Shulkin who speaks quickly is either very young or lying. I have been speaking at this pace for two hundred years.
I've read every record of every visitor to {village}. It took no time at all. The shelf was empty until you.
Driftrays nest under the bridges. If you hear something like a sail sighing below you, that is them, not the void. Usually.
Our robes are void-cloth. It is woven in the Loft from threads nobody will explain to me, and I have asked politely for sixty years.
The shellwrights say purpur remembers the hand that cut it. I say purpur is a block. We have agreed to record both views.
3: {neighbour} keeps a private ledger of who borrows what. I keep a private ledger of {neighbour}'s ledger. It's healthy, I think.
I tried to count the stars once. The Archive has the attempt: four volumes, unfinished. The last note says 'they will not hold still'.
You walk on the ground. All of it, every step, flat-footed. Doesn't it wear you out, all that touching?
Lamplighters argue about end rods the way you tell me other people argue about weather. I would love to hear one of your arguments.
First rule of the Archive: write it down. Second: write down who told you. The third is smudged. We've argued about it for a century.
A Driftray sleeps under my window. I named it Footnote. It has never once come when called. Neither do footnotes.
Chorus tastes of nothing, yes, but of nothing in eleven distinct ways. The Chorrin can tell them apart. So can I, after a century of effort.
We have no word for 'bored'. We have a word for 'between entries'. It gets a great deal of use.
When young ones misbehave, they copy out the Bylaws of the Lamp Court. All of them. Most behave beautifully afterwards. Some become archivists.
Shells darken with age. Mine was the colour of popped chorus once. Now it's the colour of a bruise, which my elder calls 'distinguished'.
The islands don't drift. But stand on a bridge long enough and you start to suspect them.
I like you, {player}, I think. I've written it down very lightly, so it can be rubbed out if need be. It hasn't been.
You keep asking questions. A good habit. The Archive is mostly questions that someone, once, bothered to answer.
6: When my lid first opened, the archivist wrote one word in my record: 'alert'. Underneath, smaller: 'if draughty'. My elders still call me Draughty.
I lost a friend to the void when I was young. A bridge, a missed step, no ray near enough. I write their name in the margin of every new volume.
Some nights I read the oldest records, from before the Long Watch. The hand is so calm. They didn't know what was coming. I envy them, and I don't.
Do you know what I'm afraid of? Not the Crowned. Not the void. An empty shelf. Something happening, and nobody writing it down.
{neighbour} and I quarrelled once, sixty years ago, over a comma. It still isn't settled. I think we both enjoy it too much.
When you're off on your travels, I check the bridge lamps more than I need to. I tell myself it's diligence.
Being Shulkin is mostly patience. We are very good at it. Sometimes I wonder if we are too good at it. We waited out a Dragon, instead of... well.
The Lid Hall seats three hundred. There are a dozen of us. We still meet there. Nobody suggests a smaller room. It would mean admitting something.
I used to think the record was the point. Lately I think the point is the person you read it to.
I once kept my lid shut for nine wakings over a broken promise. Childish. I would do it again. It was very restful.
You've seen more of the End in a year than I have in my life. I'm not jealous. I've written that down, so it's true.
There's a page in the Archive with your name on it. It's getting crowded. I've started writing smaller. I don't mind.
When I was young I wanted to be a wayfinder. Then I sat on a Driftray. It's fine. Not everyone needs to be up.
9: When I close for the last time, {player}, I'd like you to be told. Not for the record. Just so someone who knew me open knows.
I've started a private volume. Not for the Archive. Things you've said that made me laugh. It's very thin, but it's mine.
We say a Shulkin is never alone while their shell is remembered. I never believed it until lately. I think it was about friends all along.
I read your page aloud in the Nursery. The young ones booed the Dragon and cheered you. Very unprofessional of me. I'd do it again.
If the Crowned ever come for {village}, the vault key is behind the third lamp. Don't write that down. Ha. Listen to me.
The lamp I'm named for was lit by a Chorrin, passing through with a cart of chorus. We don't allow that. Nobody has ever asked me. There. Now it's said.
I used to dream of the old cities as tombs. Since you came I dream of them with the doors open. I don't know what it means. I'm glad of it.
I used to fear the day the lamps go out. Now I fear the day you don't come back over the bridge. It's a smaller fear. It's worse.
I've decided something. When the record of {village} is sealed, your name goes on the first page, not the last. The others agreed. Mostly.
You've changed how I count time. I used to count it in lamps. Now I count it in your visits. That is a very un-Shulkin thing to admit.
Everyone who ever lived in {village} is in the Archive. Lately I wonder who'll remember me. Then you knock, and I stop wondering.
I'm old enough to be tired of most things. Not of this. Not of you turning up, dusty and impossible, with a story.
Sit with me a moment and don't say anything. The lamps are humming. That's all. I wanted someone to hear it with.

0: The Dragon circled the old cities for longer than the Archive has shelves. And you silenced it. We are still learning to say that sentence calmly.
For centuries we hooded our lamps on the side facing the centre, so the Dragon would not see them. Some hoods are still on. Habit is a stubborn shell.
When it fell, every lamp in the Spire flickered at once. The lamplighters swear they had nothing to do with it.
We did not fight it. We waited. Shulkin are very good at waiting. The Dragon was very good at not leaving. It was a long contest.
3: Was it frightened, at the end? Forgive me. The Archive wants to know. So do I, which is less professional.
My elder's elder saw the Dragon loosed. They wrote one line about it, then nothing for three years. The blank pages are the worst part of the Archive.
The Crowned loosed it. Remember that, whatever they tell you. The Dragon was only the arrow. The Court drew the bow.
I'm told some of you bring it back, to fight it again. Please don't. We have only just put the hoods away.
6: I used to dream the Dragon landed on our Lamp Tower and simply looked at me. I haven't had that dream since you came. I wanted you to know.
You fought it with the crystals burning and the Unlidded watching. Alone. I couldn't have. I've thought about that a great deal.
The Archive calls you 'the one who silenced the Dragon'. I call you {player}. I'm told that's irregular. Let them tell me.
9: Sometimes I'm almost sorry for it. Bound to the Court, circling an empty city for an age. Is that strange? You're the only one I'd say it to.
When the Dragon died, we lost the thing we were waiting out. Some of us don't know what to wait for now. I wait for your visits.
If it ever came back, I'd want to be standing next to you. Not behind. Next to. Write that down for me; I'm too frightened to.

0: Work? I am between offices. The Lid Hall assures me this is an honour. I assure the Lid Hall that it is not.
I keep the Spire's general record. That is, I notice things. It is a calling with no robe and very poor pay.
I help where I'm needed. Mostly I'm needed to hold the other end of things.
The shellwrights have promised me an apprenticeship. They promised it in a very slow voice.
3: I tally the chorus deliveries from the Chorrin. Never late, never on time. They come when the fruit is ready, and the fruit won't be hurried.
Unofficially, I tell the lamplighter which rods flicker. Officially, I'm a nuisance.
I polish the Eye in the Lamp Court tiles. Every tile, every lit hour. It doesn't need it. Someone ought to do it anyway.
6: Honestly, {player}? I've never found the work that fits. Everyone else's lamp burns a certain colour. Mine just burns.
I sat a year at the archivist's elbow and a year at the weaver's loom. I was adequate at both. 'Adequate' is in my record twice.
Perhaps my work is to remember the people who do the work. Someone has to keep the keepers.
9: I think my work now is being your friend in {village}. Unpaid, unrecorded, and the best office I've held.
If you ask for nothing, they forget to give you a post, and you get to talk to visitors. That's my whole secret.
When you leave, I go to the Roost and watch the gaps until you're past them. If that's a job, I'm very good at it.

0: This island has held {village} since the Long Watch began. The bridges came later. The first generation simply did not visit each other.
Every building here is shaped like a shell: a body, a glowing gap, a lid. We build what we are. It saves on explanations.
The Lamp Tower stands tallest because light carries furthest from high up, and the dark is where the Unlidded walk in.
A Lid Hall, an Archive, a Nursery and a great many stairs. Mind the bridges. The rails are recent and nobody fully trusts them.
You'll want to meet {neighbour}. Everyone does, eventually. It's quicker than trying to avoid them.
3: {neighbour} has borrowed my second-best lamp hook for eleven years. The Archive holds the receipt. I bring it up at every festival.
We are small here, but very well documented. You could find out what anyone ate on any lit hour of the last century. Nobody ever wants to.
The Nursery is the loudest place in {village}. Young lids pop open at everything. It sounds like a kiln full of chorus.
We voted on the bridge rails. It took a decade. Meanwhile three people fell. Two were caught by Driftrays. The rails won.
6: {neighbour} pretends not to like you. They asked me three questions about you since the last bell. That's three more than they ask about anyone.
I know every creak in {village}. Lately there's a new one: yours, coming over the east bridge. I listen for it.
I've seen three lamplighters retire here. Each one said the rods were dimmer than in their day. Each one was right, slightly.
9: If {village} ever has to move, I've listed what to carry. The Archive, the young ones, the lamps. You're on it. Don't argue; it's in ink.
When I'm gone, {neighbour} will keep my shelf. I've asked them to keep a page free for you. They grumbled. That's a yes.
The whole of {village} has decided you're one of us, as much as anyone without a lid can be. There was no vote. Everyone simply started setting a place.

0: The Chorrin? Our oldest partners. Every wall here is purpur, purpur is popped chorus, and the chorus was theirs. We built our cities out of their harvests.
They hum instead of speaking. You get used to it. After a century you start humming back by accident, which they find hilarious.
We call it the Old Accord: we built, they grew. Then the Dragon came, and the Accord became a correspondence.
They blink away when startled. Vanish, and turn up a few steps over. We slam our lids. Every people has its dignity.
3: Chorrin are warm and blunt and loud. Shulkin are cool and careful and quiet. Put us in a room and it's either a feast or a treaty dispute.
I like them. Quietly. Say it aloud and they hug you, and they're made of stone, and I'm made of shell. A bad combination.
They never write anything down. They remember in songs. I've tried to record the songs. They change them on purpose, I'm sure of it.
A Chorrin once asked what I keep in my shell. I said 'myself'. They laughed for an hour. I still don't know what was funny.
6: We're equals now. Partners. The record says so. But it also remembers that, in the old cities, they lived on the lower floors. Some of them remember too.
When the Dragon came, the Chorrin hid our young in their groves. The Archive has the names. I read them every year. They don't know we do that.
I'm wary of them, a little. They're wary of us. That's honest, at least. The Crowned are never wary; they're certain. I'll take honest.
9: My oldest friend was a Chorrin. They went quiet mid-hum, at a kiln, laughing at some joke of mine. I've never dared tell it again.
If you're ever in a Stead, tell them {name} of {village} sends formal regards. They'll know what that means. It means warm ones.
The Old Accord was more than trade. Our walls were their harvests; their songs had our lamps in them. I'd like to see that again before I close.

0: The Crowned rule the Unlidded and, they believe, everything else. We disagree, quietly, from a great distance.
Do not meet the eyes of the Unlidded. It is not rude to them. It is an offence against their masters, and their masters keep long records too.
The Unlidded haul stone for the Court. That is why they carry blocks about. Nobody ever told them they could stop.
We do not speak of the Crowned after the bell. It is not superstition. It is caution with a long memory.
3: The Crowned loosed the Dragon on our cities, then sent envoys to explain why it was our fault. The Archive keeps both accounts. Only one is in good ink.
A Citadel? Stay away, unless you carry their seal. And if you carry their seal, stay away harder.
I pity the Unlidded, a little. A life where looking up is a crime. We live in shells, but at least our lids are our own.
The Court has eight-eyed lords who never sleep. We have lamps that never go out. Draw your own conclusions.
6: The Crowned won't have forgotten that you killed their Dragon. They forget nothing. In that, and only in that, they're like us.
An envoy came here once, when I was young. Tall, black, a crown of eyes. It never blinked. Every lid in {village} stayed shut until it left.
No one has ever seen an Endarch born. The Archive has a whole shelf of guesses. None of them help me sleep.
9: If the Crowned ever come for you, {player}, come here. We can't fight them. But we can shut the doors, and we are very, very good at shut.
I'm afraid of the Court. I've never said so aloud. A Shulkin is meant to record fear, not feel it. Well. Now it's recorded.
Some nights I wonder whether the Unlidded remember being anything else. Whether anyone keeps their records. I hope someone does.

0: Water falls from the sky? Unprompted? And nobody records where it lands? I'll need to sit down. Well. Hover lower.
The ground grows a green carpet by itself, and you walk on it, and it grows back. That sounds exhausting for the carpet.
A great lamp in the sky that nobody tends? Who trims it? What if it goes out? ...It goes out every evening? And everyone simply lets it?
Beasts that give drink and are eaten as well? 'Cows'. The Chorrin will be fascinated. I'm merely appalled. Efficiently appalled.
3: Villages with no lids, trading in green stones, and nobody writes anything down? How do they know what happened yesterday?
A day and a night that take turns? How does anyone agree what time it is? We barely manage, and we have a bell.
Wind. Air that moves by itself, and pushes. Tell me more about wind. No, don't. I want to imagine it a while first.
Trees? Wood that grows upright out of the ground? We have six wooden doors in {village}. Nobody knows where the wood came from. We guard them like treasure.
6: When you talk about the Overworld, your voice changes. I've noted it. It's how mine sounds when I talk about the old cities.
Is it true the sky there is blue? Not dark? I tried to imagine it and had to close for an hour.
Snow. Water that falls slowly, and white, and stays. I asked the weaver for a cloth like it. It's terrible. I love it.
Does anyone write about you, up there? Someone should. If no one does, I have a spare volume.
9: Someday I'd like to see rain. Just once. I'd hover in it with my lid wide open and not write a single word.
You'll go back up one day for good, I suppose. Tell the sun about us. Someone up there should know we kept the lamps lit.
I've started a shelf for the Overworld. Cows, rain, grass, the sun: everything you've told me. It's the most read shelf in the Archive. The young ones queue.

0: The shulkers in the old cities are our elders. A Shulkin who closes and never opens again leaves a living shell. They are still keeping the doors.
You'll have met them. They lift strangers into the air. It was always their way of asking someone to leave.
We don't go to the old cities. It would be like walking through a hall of sleeping relatives with dirty feet.
They don't speak any more. But now and then they open and look out. We think that's the last thing a Shulkin keeps: the looking.
3: The old cities were ours. Every tower. When the Dragon came, the eldest closed in the doorways so the rest of us could get away. They're still there.
Some say the closed ones dream. The Archive is divided. I hope they do. I hope it's of lamps.
If one of them shot at you, it wasn't personal. Probably. They were guarding something. Probably us.
There's a word for the moment a lid stops opening. We don't say it. We write it, and then we shut the book for a while.
6: My elder's elder is up there, I think. In a tower by the ship. I've never gone to see. I'm afraid I'd know the shell.
When a Shulkin closes for the last time, we light a lamp in their niche and leave it until it fails. Sometimes it takes years. That's the point.
In the old days the closed were carried to the cities, to keep the doors. Now there's nowhere to carry them. We keep them in the Nursery, with the young.
9: When I close, {player}, I'd like a view of the gap you cross. So I can keep watch for you. That's what we do, you see. Even after.
You've walked through their halls. Did they seem at peace? Don't spare me. I've waited all my life to ask someone who's been.
I think the old ones would have liked you. You opened their cities again. Nobody had for an age. That matters, to a shell.

0: *the lid lowers to a slit* You are carrying a shell box. Two shells, by the look of it. I will not ask whose. I suspect neither of us would like the answer.
That box on your back. I'd rather you didn't set it down in the Lamp Court. Or in front of anyone's elders. Which is everywhere.
Ah. A shulker box. How useful. How very roomy. How... *the lid closes, and does not open for some time*
I see you've brought luggage. Somebody's great-elder, by the look of the hinge.
3: You keep your tools in it. Your blocks. Your things. I know. I'm trying not to think of it as a tomb. I'm managing poorly.
I won't be cross. I'll be formal. Very, very formal. A good lit hour to you, Dragon-slayer, and to your... cargo.
Please don't open it near me. I couldn't bear the sound. The hinge of a shell sounds exactly the same, you see.
6: I know you didn't mean anything by it. Up there, a shell is just a shell. Down here it's a grandparent. Both are true, and I hate it.
Could you at least keep something decent in it? Not dirt. A book, perhaps. A lamp. Something they'd have approved of.
Whoever they were, they guarded doors. Now they guard your cobblestone. I'm trying to find a dignified way to feel about that.
9: I've made my peace with your box. Whoever it was, they're travelling now. They've seen more of the world than any of us. Perhaps that's not a bad ending.
Bring it here. Let me... *three thin fingers rest on the lid, very lightly* There. I said hello. Carry them carefully.
If my shell ends up in a box one day, I hope it's yours. I mean that kindly. You'd take me somewhere worth seeing.

0: *the lid slams shut* Those are the Crowned's eyes. Their envoys carried them. Put them away. Please. Further away than that.
Where did you get that reliquary? No. Don't tell me. If I don't know, I can't be made to say.
Whatever you mean to do with those, do it somewhere that isn't {village}. The Court's eyes see even from inside a jar.
An envoy's seal. The last time one crossed our bridges, the envoy read us new laws and the Archive gained a shelf of grief.
3: You'd go to a Citadel with those? Then they'll let you in. That's the worrying part. Getting out is a separate law.
*the lid hovers, half shut* I trust you. I don't trust anything the Crowned made. Just now those two are standing very close together.
Taken off a ship, I suppose. The Court's envoys are long gone and their seals still frighten me. That tells you something.
6: If you're going to the Court, tell me first. I'll want to write down that you went. And then I'll want to write that you came back.
Keep them wrapped, at least. I don't like to think of them looking at the lamps. Learning the Spire by heart.
I know why you carry them. You're curious. I'm curious too; that's why I'm frightened. Curious people walk into Citadels.
9: Come back from the Citadel. That's all I ask. And keep the eyes on you every step, or their guest-law ends where you stand.
Don't let them keep you. The Court collects things. I would like you to remain uncollected.
*the lid stays open, though it trembles* I'm not closing. Not with you. Even with those. That's how much you've changed me.
If they ask about us, tell them nothing. Tell them we're dull. We are, a little. It's our best defence.

0: Something has shifted. I'll record it once I've decided what to call it.
I've moved your entry up the page. A small thing. In the Archive, not a small thing at all.
1: I've written your name in the margin. Margins are where the Archive keeps the interesting things.
You've been promoted from 'visitor' to 'returning visitor'. There's no ceremony. I'm holding a small one in my head.
2: You're a footnote now. Don't look like that. Footnotes are where the truth hides from people who skim.
I've added a footnote under the Dragon entry. Small print. It says only: 'and then they came back to visit'.
3: Your name has its own line in my ledger now. Not shared with deliveries or lamp repairs. Its own line.
*the lid lifts a little higher than before, and stays there* I find I'm less careful around you. Interesting.
4: I've stopped writing 'the Dragon-slayer'. From now on it's {player}, in full, every time. It takes longer. Worth the ink.
I told {neighbour} about you without being asked. That has never happened before. They looked alarmed.
5: I've given you a page of your own. Blank, mostly. I wanted to leave room for whatever comes.
A whole page, {player}. Most Shulkin wait a century for a page. Don't let it go to your shell. Oh. You haven't one.
6: You're cross-referenced now. Your page points to mine and mine to yours. In the Archive, that's how you say 'friends'.
I found you in three other people's records. {neighbour} spelt your name wrong. I've corrected it. Kindly.
7: I've had your pages bound. Proper void-cloth covers. Don't make a fuss. Or do, a small one; I'd like to see it.
You've a volume now. A real one, on a real shelf. I keep going to look at it. That's not normal behaviour for me.
8: I've moved your volume to the shelf by the lamp, where the light is best. Where I can find it in the dark.
You may call me by my lamp now. Friends do. It was the last lamp in the row, the one that always guttered. Not grand. Mine.
9: I've moved your volume into the vault, with the oldest records. It's where we keep what we cannot bear to lose.
Only the oldest records go into the vault. And now yours. The oldest records won't mind. I asked.
